chapters.content:
CHAPTER 1. Scene IAct Ihttps://standardebooks.org/ebooks/william-shakespeare/henry-vi-part-iii/text/act-1#scene-1-1

London. The Parliament-house.

Alarum. Enter the Duke of York, Edward, Richard, Norfolk, Montague, Warwick, and Soldiers.

Warwick I wonder how the king escaped our hands.

York

While we pursued the horsemen of the north,

He slyly stole away and left his men:

Whereat the great Lord of Northumberland,

Whose warlike ears could never brook retreat,

Cheer'd up the drooping army; and himself,

Lord Clifford and Lord Stafford, all abreast,

Charged our main battle's front, and breaking in

Were by the swords of common soldiers slain.

Edward

Lord Stafford's father, Duke of Buckingham,

Is either slain or wounded dangerously;

I cleft his beaver with a downright blow:

That this is true, father, behold his blood.

Montague

And, brother, here's the Earl of Wiltshire's blood,

Whom I encounter'd as the battles join'd.

Richard Speak thou for me and tell them what I did. Throwing down the Duke of Somerset's head.

York

Richard hath best deserved of all my sons.

But is your grace dead, my Lord of Somerset?

Norfolk Such hope have all the line of John of Gaunt!

Richard Thus do I hope to shake King Henry's head.

Warwick

And so do I. Victorious Prince of York,

Before I see thee seated in that throne

Which now the house of Lancaster usurps,

I vow by heaven these eyes shall never close.

This is the palace of the fearful king,

And this the regal seat: possess it, York;

For this is thine and not King Henry's heirs'.

York

Assist me, then, sweet Warwick, and I will;

For hither we have broken in by force.

Norfolk We'll all assist you; he that flies shall die.

York

Thanks, gentle Norfolk: stay by me, my lords;

And, soldiers, stay and lodge by me this night. They go up.

Warwick

And when the king comes, offer him no violence,

Unless he seek to thrust you out perforce.

York

The queen this day here holds her parliament,

But little thinks we shall be of her council:

By words or blows here let us win our right.

Richard Arm'd as we are, let's stay within this house.

Warwick

The bloody parliament shall this be call'd,

Unless Plantagenet, Duke of York, be king,

And bashful Henry deposed, whose cowardice

Hath made us by-words to our enemies.

York

Then leave me not, my lords; be resolute;

I mean to take possession of my right.

Warwick

Neither the king, nor he that loves him best,

The proudest he that holds up Lancaster,

Dares stir a wing, if Warwick shake his bells.

I'll plant Plantagenet, root him up who dares:

Resolve thee, Richard; claim the English crown.

Flourish. Enter King Henry, Clifford, Northumberland, Westmoreland, Exeter, and the rest.

King Henry

My lords, look where the sturdy rebel sits,

Even in the chair of state: belike he means,

Back'd by the power of Warwick, that false peer,

To aspire unto the crown and reign as king.

Earl of Northumberland, he slew thy father,

And thine, Lord Clifford; and you both have vow'd revenge

On him, his sons, his favourites and his friends.

Northumberland If I be not, heavens be revenged on me!

Clifford The hope thereof makes Clifford mourn in steel.

Westmoreland

What, shall we suffer this? let's pluck him down:

My heart for anger burns; I cannot brook it.

King Henry Be patient, gentle Earl of Westmoreland.

Clifford

Patience is for poltroons, such as he:

He durst not sit there, had your father lived.

My gracious lord, here in the parliament

Let us assail the family of York.

Northumberland Well hast thou spoken, cousin: be it so.

King Henry

Ah, know you not the city favours them,

And they have troops of soldiers at their beck?

Exeter But when the duke is slain, they'll quickly fly.

King Henry

Far be the thought of this from Henry's heart,

To make a shambles of the parliament-house!

Cousin of Exeter, frowns, words and threats

Shall be the war that Henry means to use.

Thou factious Duke of York, descend my throne,

and kneel for grace and mercy at my feet;

I am thy sovereign.

York I am thine.

Exeter For shame, come down: he made thee Duke of York.

York
'Twas my inheritance, as the earldom was.

Exeter Thy father was a traitor to the crown.

Warwick

Exeter, thou art a traitor to the crown

In following this usurping Henry.

Clifford Whom should he follow but his natural king?

Warwick True, Clifford; and that's Richard Duke of York.

King Henry And shall I stand, and thou sit in my throne?

York It must and shall be so: content thyself.

Warwick Be Duke of Lancaster; let him be king.

Westmoreland

He is both king and Duke of Lancaster;

And that the Lord of Westmoreland shall maintain.

Warwick

And Warwick shall disprove it. You forget

That we are those which chased you from the field

And slew your fathers, and with colours spread

March'd through the city to the palace gates.

Northumberland

Yes, Warwick, I remember it to my grief;

And, by his soul, thou and thy house shall rue it.

Westmoreland

Plantagenet, of thee and these thy sons,

Thy kinsman and thy friends, I'll have more lives

Than drops of blood were in my father's veins.

Clifford

Urge it no more; lest that, instead of words,

I send thee, Warwick, such a messenger

As shall revenge his death before I stir.

Warwick Poor Clifford! how I scorn his worthless threats!

York

Will you we show our title to the crown?

If not, our swords shall plead it in the field.

King Henry

What title hast thou, traitor, to the crown?

Thy father was, as thou art, Duke of York;

Thy grandfather, Roger Mortimer, Earl of March:

I am the son of Henry the Fifth,

Who made the Dauphin and the French to stoop

And seized upon their towns and provinces.

Warwick Talk not of France, sith thou hast lost it all.

King Henry

The lord protector lost it, and not I:

When I was crown'd I was but nine months old.

Richard

You are old enough now, and yet, methinks, you lose.

Father, tear the crown from the usurper's head.

Edward Sweet father, do so; set it on your head.

Montague

Good brother, as thou lovest and honourest arms,

Let's fight it out and not stand cavilling thus.

Richard Sound drums and trumpets, and the king will fly.

York Sons, peace!

King Henry Peace, thou! and give King Henry leave to speak.

Warwick

Plantagenet shall speak first: hear him, lords;

And be you silent and attentive too,

For he that interrupts him shall not live.

King Henry

Think'st thou that I will leave my kingly throne,

Wherein my grandsire and my father sat?

No: first shall war unpeople this my realm;

Ay, and their colours, often borne in France,

And now in England to our heart's great sorrow,

Shall be my winding-sheet. Why faint you, lords?

My title's good, and better far than his.

Warwick Prove it, Henry, and thou shalt be king.

King Henry Henry the Fourth by conquest got the crown.

York
'Twas by rebellion against his king.

King Henry

Aside. I know not what to say; my title's weak.⁠--

Tell me, may not a king adopt an heir?

York What then?

King Henry

An if he may, then am I lawful king;

For Richard, in the view of many lords,

Resign'd the crown to Henry the Fourth,

Whose heir my father was, and I am his.

York

He rose against him, being his sovereign,

And made him to resign his crown perforce.

Warwick

Suppose, my lords, he did it unconstrain'd,

Think you 'twere prejudicial to his crown?

Exeter

No; for he could not so resign his crown

But that the next heir should succeed and reign.

King Henry Art thou against us, Duke of Exeter?

Exeter His is the right, and therefore pardon me.

York Why whisper you, my lords, and answer not?

Exeter My conscience tells me he is lawful king.

King Henry Aside. All will revolt from me, and turn to him.

Northumberland

Plantagenet, for all the claim thou lay'st,

Think not that Henry shall be so deposed.

Warwick Deposed he shall be, in despite of all.

Northumberland

Thou art deceived: 'tis not thy southern power,

Of Essex, Norfolk, Suffolk, nor of Kent,

Which makes thee thus presumptuous and proud,

Can set the duke up in despite of me.

Clifford

King Henry, be thy title right or wrong,

Lord Clifford vows to fight in thy defence:

May that ground gape and swallow me alive,

Where I shall kneel to him that slew my father!

King Henry O Clifford, how thy words revive my heart!

York

Henry of Lancaster, resign thy crown.

What mutter you, or what conspire you, lords?

Warwick

Do right unto this princely Duke of York,

Or I will fill the house with armed men,

And over the chair of state, where now he sits,

Write up his title with usurping blood. He stamps with his foot, and the Soldiers show themselves.

King Henry

My Lord of Warwick, hear me but one word:

Let me for this my life-time reign as king.

York

Confirm the crown to me and to mine heirs,

And thou shalt reign in quiet while thou livest.

King Henry

I am content: Richard Plantagenet,

Enjoy the kingdom after my decease.

Clifford What wrong is this unto the prince your son!

Warwick What good is this to England and himself!

Westmoreland Base, fearful and despairing Henry!

Clifford How hast thou injured both thyself and us!

Westmoreland I cannot stay to hear these articles.

Northumberland Nor I.

Clifford Come, cousin, let us tell the queen these news.

Westmoreland

Farewell, faint-hearted and degenerate king,

In whose cold blood no spark of honour bides.

Northumberland

Be thou a prey unto the house of York,

And die in bands for this unmanly deed!

Clifford

In dreadful war mayst thou be overcome,

Or live in peace abandon'd and despised! Exeunt Northumberland, Clifford, and Westmoreland.

Warwick Turn this way, Henry, and regard them not.

Exeter They seek revenge and therefore will not yield.

King Henry Ah, Exeter!

Warwick Why should you sigh, my lord?

King Henry

Not for myself, Lord Warwick, but my son,

Whom I unnaturally shall disinherit.

But be it as it may: I here entail

The crown to thee and to thine heirs for ever;

Conditionally, that here thou take an oath

To cease this civil war, and, whilst I live,

To honour me as thy king and sovereign,

And neither by treason nor hostility

To seek to put me down and reign thyself.

York This oath I willingly take and will perform.

Warwick Long live King Henry! Plantagenet, embrace him.

King Henry And long live thou and these thy forward sons!

York Now York and Lancaster are reconciled.

Exeter Accursed be he that seeks to make them foes! Sennet. Here they come down.

York Farewell, my gracious lord; I'll to my castle.

Warwick And I'll keep London with my soldiers.

Norfolk And I to Norfolk with my followers.

Montague And I unto the sea from whence I came. Exeunt York and his Sons, Warwick, Norfolk, Montague, their Soldiers, and Attendants.

King Henry And I, with grief and sorrow, to the court.

Enter Queen Margaret and the Prince of Whales.

Exeter

Here comes the queen, whose looks bewray her anger:

I'll steal away.

King Henry Exeter, so will I.

Queen Margaret Nay, go not from me; I will follow thee.

King Henry Be patient, gentle queen, and I will stay.

Queen Margaret

Who can be patient in such extremes?

Ah, wretched man! would I had died a maid,

And never seen thee, never borne thee son,

Seeing thou hast proved so unnatural a father!

Hath he deserved to lose his birthright thus?

Hadst thou but loved him half so well as I,

Or felt that pain which I did for him once,

Or nourish'd him as I did with my blood,

Thou wouldst have left thy dearest heart-blood there,

Rather than have that savage duke thine heir

And disinherited thine only son.

Prince

Father, you cannot disinherit me:

If you be king, why should not I succeed?

King Henry

Pardon me, Margaret; pardon me, sweet son:

The Earl of Warwick and the duke enforced me.

Queen Margaret

Enforced thee! art thou king, and wilt be forced?

I shame to hear thee speak. Ah, timorous wretch!

Thou hast undone thyself, thy son and me;

And given unto the house of York such head

As thou shalt reign but by their sufferance.

To entail him and his heirs unto the crown,

What is it, but to make thy sepulchre

And creep into it far before thy time?

Warwick is chancellor and the lord of Calais;

Stern Falconbridge commands the narrow seas;

The duke is made protector of the realm;

And yet shalt thou be safe? such safety finds

The trembling lamb environed with wolves.

Had I been there, which am a silly woman,

The soldiers should have toss'd me on their pikes

Before I would have granted to that act.

But thou preferr'st thy life before thine honour:

And seeing thou dost, I here divorce myself

Both from thy table, Henry, and thy bed,

Until that act of parliament be repeal'd

Whereby my son is disinherited.

The northern lords that have forsworn thy colours

Will follow mine, if once they see them spread;

And spread they shall be, to thy foul disgrace

And utter ruin of the house of York.

Thus do I leave thee. Come, son, let's away;

Our army is ready; come, we'll after them.

King Henry Stay, gentle Margaret, and hear me speak.

Queen Margaret Thou hast spoke too much already: get thee gone.

King Henry Gentle son Edward, thou wilt stay with me?

Queen Margaret Ay, to be murder'd by his enemies.

Prince

When I return with victory from the field

I'll see your grace: till then I'll follow her.

Queen Margaret Come, son, away; we may not linger thus. Exeunt Queen Margaret and the Prince.

King Henry

Poor queen! how love to me and to her son

Hath made her break out into terms of rage!

Revenged may she be on that hateful duke,

Whose haughty spirit, winged with desire,

Will cost my crown, and like an empty eagle

Tire on the flesh of me and of my son!

The loss of those three lords torments my heart:

I'll write unto them and entreat them fair.

Come, cousin, you shall be the messenger.

Exeter And I, I hope, shall reconcile them all. Exeunt.

questions.question: How did King Henry escape the battle, by York’s account?
questions.questionKo: 요크의 말에 따르면 헨리 왕은 어떻게 전장을 빠져나갔는가?

options.text: While they pursued the horsemen of the north, he slyly stole away and left his men.
options.textKo: 요크 쪽이 북쪽 기병을 뒤쫓는 사이, 왕은 슬그머니 빠져나가 제 군사를 버려두고 갔다.

options.text: Warwick let him pass out of pity.
options.textKo: 워릭이 가엾이 여겨 놓아주었다.

options.text: Northumberland carried him from the field wounded.
options.textKo: 노섬벌랜드가 부상한 그를 전장에서 업고 나갔다.

options.text: He was never at the battle at all.
options.textKo: 애초에 전투에 나오지 않았다.

questions.sourceSnippet: He slyly stole away and left his men

questions.question: How does Richard show what he did in the battle?
questions.questionKo: 리처드는 전투에서 한 일을 어떻게 보여 주는가?

options.text: He shows a banner taken from Clifford.
options.textKo: 클리퍼드에게서 빼앗은 군기를 보인다.

options.text: He throws down the Duke of Somerset’s head and says "Speak thou for me and tell them what I did."
options.textKo: 서머싯 공의 머리를 내던지며 "네가 나를 대신해 말하고 내가 한 일을 일러라" 라고 한다.

options.text: He displays his own wounds to his father.
options.textKo: 제 상처를 아버지에게 내보인다.

options.text: He says nothing, leaving Edward to speak for him.
options.textKo: 아무 말 없이 에드워드가 대신 말하게 둔다.

questions.sourceSnippet: Speak thou for me and tell them what I did.

questions.question: Why does King Henry refuse to attack York in the parliament-house?
questions.questionKo: 헨리 왕은 왜 의사당에서 요크를 치기를 거부하는가?

options.text: Because he is outnumbered and must wait for the queen.
options.textKo: 수적으로 열세라 왕비를 기다려야 하므로.

options.text: Because Exeter has forbidden it by law.
options.textKo: 엑서터가 법으로 금했으므로.

options.text: Far be the thought from Henry’s heart to make a shambles of the parliament-house — frowns, words and threats shall be the war he means to use.
options.textKo: 의사당을 도살장으로 만드는 생각은 헨리의 마음에서 멀다며 — 찌푸림과 말과 위협만을 전쟁의 수단으로 삼겠다고.

options.text: Because Clifford and Northumberland have deserted him.
options.textKo: 클리퍼드와 노섬벌랜드가 그를 버렸으므로.

questions.sourceSnippet: To make a shambles of the parliament-house!

questions.question: What claim does King Henry make for his own title?
questions.questionKo: 헨리 왕이 제 왕위 계승권에 대해 내세우는 주장은?

options.text: That Parliament elected him and may not unmake him.
options.textKo: 의회가 자기를 뽑았으니 되돌릴 수 없다는 것.

options.text: That he was crowned by the Pope himself.
options.textKo: 교황이 직접 대관해 주었다는 것.

options.text: That York’s grandfather resigned all claim in writing.
options.textKo: 요크의 조부가 서면으로 모든 권리를 포기했다는 것.

options.text: He is the son of Henry the Fifth, who made the Dauphin and the French to stoop and seized their towns and provinces.
options.textKo: 자기는 황태자와 프랑스인들을 굴복시키고 그 도시와 지방을 차지한 헨리 5세의 아들이라는 것.

questions.sourceSnippet: I am the son of Henry the Fifth

questions.question: What does King Henry admit to himself in an aside?
questions.questionKo: 헨리 왕이 방백으로 스스로 인정하는 것은?

options.text: "I know not what to say; my title’s weak" — and later, "All will revolt from me, and turn to him."
options.textKo: "무슨 말을 해야 할지 모르겠다 — 내 권리가 약하다" 그리고 뒤에는 "모두가 나를 버리고 그에게 돌아서겠구나."

options.text: That he will fight to the last man for the crown.
options.textKo: 왕관을 위해 마지막 한 사람까지 싸우겠다고.

options.text: That Exeter has betrayed him to York.
options.textKo: 엑서터가 자기를 요크에게 팔아넘겼다고.

options.text: That he never wished to be king at all.
options.textKo: 애초에 왕이 되고 싶지 않았다고.

questions.sourceSnippet: I know not what to say; my title’s weak

questions.question: What settlement do Henry and York reach?
questions.questionKo: 헨리와 요크가 이르는 타협은?

options.text: York withdraws his claim entirely in exchange for Calais.
options.textKo: 요크가 칼레를 받는 대가로 주장을 완전히 거둔다.

options.text: Henry reigns for his lifetime and entails the crown to York and his heirs after his decease — York swearing to cease the civil war and honour Henry while he lives.
options.textKo: 헨리가 살아 있는 동안 다스리고 죽은 뒤 왕관을 요크와 그 후손에게 물려주기로 — 요크는 내전을 그치고 헨리가 사는 동안 그를 왕으로 받들겠다 맹세한다.

options.text: Henry abdicates at once and retires to a monastery.
options.textKo: 헨리가 즉시 퇴위하고 수도원으로 물러난다.

options.text: They agree to divide the kingdom between them.
options.textKo: 왕국을 둘로 나누기로 한다.

questions.sourceSnippet: I here entail The crown to thee and to thine heirs for ever

questions.question: How do Northumberland, Clifford and Westmoreland react to the settlement?
questions.questionKo: 노섬벌랜드·클리퍼드·웨스트모얼랜드는 그 타협에 어떻게 반응하는가?

options.text: They swear allegiance to York on the spot.
options.textKo: 그 자리에서 요크에게 충성을 맹세한다.

options.text: They praise Henry’s wisdom in avoiding war.
options.textKo: 전쟁을 피한 헨리의 지혜를 칭송한다.

options.text: They will not stay to hear the articles — they leave cursing him as a faint-hearted and degenerate king, and go to tell the queen.
options.textKo: 조항을 끝까지 듣지도 않고 — 겁 많고 타락한 왕이라 저주하며 자리를 떠 왕비에게 알리러 간다.

options.text: They ask for time to consider and remain.
options.textKo: 생각할 시간을 청하며 남는다.

questions.sourceSnippet: Farewell, faint-hearted and degenerate king

questions.question: What does Queen Margaret declare when she hears of the entail?
questions.questionKo: 왕비 마거릿은 그 상속 약정을 듣고 무엇을 선언하는가?

options.text: That she accepts the settlement for the sake of peace.
options.textKo: 평화를 위해 그 타협을 받아들이겠다고.

options.text: That she will take the prince to France for safety.
options.textKo: 안전을 위해 왕자를 프랑스로 데려가겠다고.

options.text: That she will appeal to Parliament to reverse it.
options.textKo: 의회에 호소해 뒤집겠다고.

options.text: She divorces herself from Henry’s table and bed until the act is repealed — and will spread the northern lords’ colours to the ruin of the house of York.
options.textKo: 그 법령이 폐기될 때까지 헨리의 식탁과 침상에서 스스로를 갈라놓겠다고 — 그리고 북쪽 귀족들의 깃발을 펼쳐 요크 가문을 무너뜨리겠다고.

chapters.content:
CHAPTER 2. Scene IIAct Ihttps://standardebooks.org/ebooks/william-shakespeare/henry-vi-part-iii/text/act-1#scene-1-2

Sandal Castle.

Enter Richard, Edward, and Montague.

Richard Brother, though I be youngest, give me leave.

Edward No, I can better play the orator.

Montague But I have reasons strong and forcible.

Enter the Duke of York.

York

Why, how now, sons and brother! at a strife?

What is your quarrel? how began it first?

Edward No quarrel, but a slight contention.

York About what?

Richard

About that which concerns your grace and us;

The crown of England, father, which is yours.

York Mine boy? not till King Henry be dead.

Richard Your right depends not on his life or death.

Edward

Now you are heir, therefore enjoy it now:

By giving the house of Lancaster leave to breathe,

It will outrun you, father, in the end.

York I took an oath that he should quietly reign.

Edward

But for a kingdom any oath may be broken:

I would break a thousand oaths to reign one year.

Richard No; God forbid your grace should be forsworn.

York I shall be, if I claim by open war.

Richard I'll prove the contrary, if you'll hear me speak.

York Thou canst not, son; it is impossible.

Richard

An oath is of no moment, being not took

Before a true and lawful magistrate,

That hath authority over him that swears:

Henry had none, but did usurp the place;

Then, seeing 'twas he that made you to depose,

Your oath, my lord, is vain and frivolous.

Therefore, to arms! And, father, do but think

How sweet a thing it is to wear a crown;

Within whose circuit is Elysium

And all that poets feign of bliss and joy.

Why do we finger thus? I cannot rest

Until the white rose that I wear be dyed

Even in the lukewarm blood of Henry's heart.

York

Richard, enough; I will be king, or die.

Brother, thou shalt to London presently,

And whet on Warwick to this enterprise.

Thou, Richard, shalt to the Duke of Norfolk,

And tell him privily of our intent.

You, Edward, shall unto my Lord Cobham,

With whom the Kentishmen will willingly rise:

In them I trust; for they are soldiers,

Witty, courteous, liberal, full of spirit.

While you are thus employ'd, what resteth more,

But that I seek occasion how to rise,

And yet the king not privy to my drift,

Nor any of the house of Lancaster?

Enter a Messenger.

But, stay: what news? Why comest thou in such post?

Messenger

The queen with all the northern earls and lords

Intend here to besiege you in your castle:

She is hard by with twenty thousand men;

And therefore fortify your hold, my lord.

York

Ay, with my sword. What! think'st thou that we fear them?

Edward and Richard, you shall stay with me;

My brother Montague shall post to London:

Let noble Warwick, Cobham, and the rest,

Whom we have left protectors of the king,

With powerful policy strengthen themselves,

And trust not simple Henry nor his oaths.

Montague

Brother, I go; I'll win them, fear it not:

And thus most humbly I do take my leave. Exit.

Enter Sir John Mortimer and Sir Hugh Mortimer.

York

Sir John and Sir Hugh Mortimer, mine uncles,

You are come to Sandal in a happy hour;

The army of the queen mean to besiege us.

Sir John She shall not need; we'll meet her in the field.

York What, with five thousand men?

Richard

Ay, with five hundred, father, for a need:

A woman's general; what should we fear? A march afar off.

Edward

I hear their drums: let's set our men in order,

And issue forth and bid them battle straight.

York

Five men to twenty! though the odds be great,

I doubt not, uncle, of our victory.

Many a battle have I won in France,

When as the enemy hath been ten to one:

Why should I not now have the like success? Alarum. Exeunt.

questions.question: What are York’s sons arguing about when he enters?
questions.questionKo: 요크가 들어섰을 때 그 아들들이 다투고 있던 것은?

options.text: Which of them shall speak — about that which concerns them all: the crown of England, which Richard says is their father’s.
options.textKo: 누가 말할 것인가 — 모두에게 관계된 일, 곧 리처드가 아버지의 것이라 말하는 잉글랜드의 왕관에 대하여.

options.text: Which of them fought best at the last battle.
options.textKo: 지난 전투에서 누가 가장 잘 싸웠는가.

options.text: Whether to fortify Sandal Castle or abandon it.
options.textKo: 샌들성을 요새로 만들 것인가 버릴 것인가.

options.text: Who shall carry the message to Warwick in London.
options.textKo: 런던의 워릭에게 누가 전갈을 가져갈 것인가.

questions.sourceSnippet: The crown of England, father, which is yours

questions.question: What objection does York raise to claiming the crown now?
questions.questionKo: 요크가 지금 왕관을 주장하는 데 대해 내놓는 반대는?

options.text: That his army is too small to face the queen.
options.textKo: 군대가 왕비를 대적하기에 너무 적다고.

options.text: He took an oath that Henry should quietly reign — and would be forsworn if he claimed by open war.
options.textKo: 헨리가 조용히 다스리게 하겠다고 맹세했으므로 — 공공연한 전쟁으로 주장하면 맹세를 어기는 것이 된다고.

options.text: That the city of London will not support him.
options.textKo: 런던시가 그를 지지하지 않으리라고.

options.text: That his sons are too young for such a war.
options.textKo: 아들들이 그런 전쟁을 치르기엔 너무 어리다고.

questions.sourceSnippet: I took an oath that he should quietly reign

questions.question: How does Edward answer that objection, and how does Richard differ?
questions.questionKo: 에드워드는 그 반대에 어떻게 답하며, 리처드는 어떻게 다른가?

options.text: Both agree the oath must be kept at all costs.
options.textKo: 둘 다 무슨 일이 있어도 맹세를 지켜야 한다고 한다.

options.text: Both urge him to ask the Pope for a dispensation.
options.textKo: 둘 다 교황에게 면제를 청하라 권한다.

options.text: Edward says for a kingdom any oath may be broken; Richard says God forbid his grace should be forsworn, and undertakes to prove the oath void instead.
options.textKo: 에드워드는 왕국을 위해서라면 어떤 맹세든 깨도 된다 하고, 리처드는 아버지가 맹세를 어겨서는 안 된다며 대신 그 맹세가 무효임을 증명하겠다고 한다.

options.text: Edward says nothing; Richard urges patience.
options.textKo: 에드워드는 말이 없고 리처드는 인내를 권한다.

questions.sourceSnippet: But for a kingdom any oath may be broken

questions.question: What is Richard’s argument that the oath does not bind?
questions.questionKo: 그 맹세가 구속력이 없다는 리처드의 논거는?

options.text: That an oath sworn under armed threat is void.
options.textKo: 무력의 위협 아래 한 맹세는 무효라는 것.

options.text: That York swore only for himself, not for his heirs.
options.textKo: 요크는 자기 몫만 맹세했지 후손 몫은 아니라는 것.

options.text: That Warwick swore it in his stead.
options.textKo: 워릭이 그를 대신해 맹세했다는 것.

options.text: An oath is of no moment, not being taken before a true and lawful magistrate with authority over him that swears — and Henry usurped the place.
options.textKo: 맹세하는 자에 대해 권한을 지닌 참되고 적법한 관헌 앞에서 한 것이 아니면 아무 무게가 없는데 — 헨리는 그 자리를 찬탈했다는 것.

questions.sourceSnippet: An oath is of no moment, being not took Before a true and lawful magistrate

questions.question: How does Richard describe the wearing of a crown?
questions.questionKo: 리처드는 왕관을 쓰는 일을 어떻게 말하는가?

options.text: Within whose circuit is Elysium and all that poets feign of bliss and joy.
options.textKo: 그 테두리 안에 엘리시온이 있고, 시인들이 지어낸 온갖 지복과 기쁨이 다 들어 있다고.

options.text: That it is a burden heavier than any armour.
options.textKo: 어떤 갑옷보다 무거운 짐이라고.

options.text: That it brings only sleepless nights and enemies.
options.textKo: 잠 못 드는 밤과 적들만 가져온다고.

options.text: That it is worth less than a good sword.
options.textKo: 좋은 칼 한 자루보다 값이 못하다고.

questions.sourceSnippet: Within whose circuit is Elysium

questions.question: What errands does York give once he resolves?
questions.questionKo: 결심한 요크가 내리는 심부름은?

options.text: All three to raise the Kentishmen together.
options.textKo: 셋 모두 함께 켄트 사람들을 일으키러.

options.text: Montague to London to whet on Warwick, Richard to the Duke of Norfolk, and Edward to Lord Cobham — with whom the Kentishmen will willingly rise.
options.textKo: 몬터규는 런던으로 가 워릭을 부추기고, 리처드는 노퍽 공에게, 에드워드는 켄트 사람들이 기꺼이 일어설 코범 경에게.

options.text: Richard to the king, to ask for a truce.
options.textKo: 리처드는 왕에게 휴전을 청하러.

options.text: Edward to France, to seek the Dauphin’s aid.
options.textKo: 에드워드는 프랑스로 황태자의 원조를 구하러.

questions.sourceSnippet: You, Edward, shall unto my Lord Cobham, With whom the Kentishmen will willingly rise

questions.question: What news does the messenger bring to Sandal Castle?
questions.questionKo: 전령이 샌들성에 가져온 소식은?

options.text: That Warwick has been defeated in London.
options.textKo: 워릭이 런던에서 패했다는 것.

options.text: That King Henry has repealed the act of parliament.
options.textKo: 헨리 왕이 그 의회 법령을 폐기했다는 것.

options.text: The queen with all the northern earls and lords intends to besiege them — she is hard by with twenty thousand men.
options.textKo: 왕비가 북쪽의 백작과 귀족을 모두 이끌고 포위하려 한다는 것 — 2만 병력과 함께 코앞까지 왔다.

options.text: That the Kentishmen refuse to rise.
options.textKo: 켄트 사람들이 일어나기를 거부한다는 것.

questions.sourceSnippet: She is hard by with twenty thousand men

questions.question: How does York answer the odds against him?
questions.questionKo: 요크는 불리한 병력 차이에 어떻게 답하는가?

options.text: He orders the gates barred and refuses battle.
options.textKo: 성문을 걸어 잠그고 싸움을 거부한다.

options.text: He sends to Warwick for reinforcements first.
options.textKo: 먼저 워릭에게 지원군을 청한다.

options.text: He proposes to treat with the queen.
options.textKo: 왕비와 담판하자고 제안한다.

options.text: Five men to twenty, and yet he doubts not of victory — for he won many a battle in France when the enemy was ten to one.
options.textKo: 스물에 다섯이라도 승리를 의심하지 않는다고 — 프랑스에서 열 배의 적을 상대로도 여러 번 이겼으므로.

questions.sourceSnippet: Many a battle have I won in France, When as the enemy hath been ten to one

chapters.content:
CHAPTER 3. Scene IIIAct Ihttps://standardebooks.org/ebooks/william-shakespeare/henry-vi-part-iii/text/act-1#scene-1-3

Field of battle betwixt Sandal Castle and Wakefield.

Alarums. Enter Rutland and his Tutor.

Rutland

Ah, whither shall I fly to 'scape their hands?

Ah, tutor, look where bloody Clifford comes!

Enter Clifford and Soldiers.

Clifford

Chaplain, away! thy priesthood saves thy life.

As for the brat of this accursed duke,

Whose father slew my father, he shall die.

Tutor And I, my lord, will bear him company.

Clifford Soldiers, away with him!

Tutor

Ah, Clifford, murder not this innocent child,

Lest thou be hated both of God and man! Exit, dragged off by Soldiers.

Clifford

How now! is he dead already? or is it fear

That makes him close his eyes? I'll open them.

Rutland

So looks the pent-up lion o'er the wretch

That trembles under his devouring paws;

And so he walks, insulting o'er his prey,

And so he comes, to rend his limbs asunder.

Ah, gentle Clifford, kill me with thy sword,

And not with such a cruel threatening look.

Sweet Clifford, hear me speak before I die.

I am too mean a subject for thy wrath:

Be thou revenged on men, and let me live.

Clifford

In vain thou speak'st, poor boy; my father's blood

Hath stopp'd the passage where thy words should enter.

Rutland

Then let my father's blood open it again:

He is a man, and, Clifford, cope with him.

Clifford

Had thy brethren here, their lives and thine

Were not revenge sufficient for me;

No, if I digg'd up thy forefathers' graves

And hung their rotten coffins up in chains,

It could not slake mine ire, nor ease my heart.

The sight of any of the house of York

Is as a fury to torment my soul;

And till I root out their accursed line

And leave not one alive, I live in hell.

Therefore⁠--Lifting his hand.

Rutland

O, let me pray before I take my death!

To thee I pray; sweet Clifford, pity me!

Clifford Such pity as my rapier's point affords.

Rutland I never did thee harm: why wilt thou slay me?

Clifford Thy father hath.

Rutland

But 'twas ere I was born.

Thou hast one son; for his sake pity me,

Lest in revenge thereof, sith God is just,

He be as miserably slain as I.

Ah, let me live in prison all my days;

And when I give occasion of offence,

Then let me die, for now thou hast no cause.

Clifford

No cause!

Thy father slew my father; therefore, die. Stabs him.

Rutland

Di faciant laudis summa sit ista tuae!
Dies.

Clifford

Plantagenet! I come, Plantagenet!

And this thy son's blood cleaving to my blade

Shall rust upon my weapon, till thy blood,

Congeal'd with this, do make me wipe off both. Exit.

questions.question: Why does Clifford spare the Tutor?
questions.questionKo: 클리퍼드는 왜 가정교사를 살려 주는가?

options.text: His priesthood saves his life — "Chaplain, away!"
options.textKo: 사제의 신분이 그 목숨을 구한다 — "사제여, 물러가라!"

options.text: Because the Tutor pleads his own innocence.
options.textKo: 가정교사가 자기 결백을 호소하기 때문에.

options.text: Because his soldiers refuse to touch a churchman.
options.textKo: 병사들이 성직자에게 손대기를 거부하기 때문에.

options.text: He does not spare him — the Tutor dies first.
options.textKo: 살려 주지 않는다 — 가정교사가 먼저 죽는다.

questions.sourceSnippet: Chaplain, away! thy priesthood saves thy life

questions.question: What image does Rutland use for Clifford?
questions.questionKo: 러틀랜드는 클리퍼드를 어떤 심상으로 그리는가?

options.text: A winter storm that strips the trees bare.
options.textKo: 나무를 발가벗기는 겨울 폭풍.

options.text: The pent-up lion looking over the wretch that trembles under his devouring paws, walking and insulting over his prey.
options.textKo: 집어삼킬 앞발 아래 떠는 가엾은 것을 내려다보는 갇혀 있던 사자 — 먹잇감 위를 거닐며 조롱하는.

options.text: A judge who has already written his verdict.
options.textKo: 이미 판결문을 써 둔 재판관.

options.text: A hunter who has lost his own quarry.
options.textKo: 제 사냥감을 놓친 사냥꾼.

questions.sourceSnippet: So looks the pent-up lion o’er the wretch

questions.question: Why does Clifford say Rutland’s words cannot reach him?
questions.questionKo: 클리퍼드는 왜 러틀랜드의 말이 자기에게 닿을 수 없다고 하는가?

options.text: Because he has sworn an oath never to hear a York.
options.textKo: 요크 사람의 말은 듣지 않겠다 맹세했으므로.

options.text: Because the alarums are too loud to hear.
options.textKo: 전투의 소음이 너무 커서 들리지 않으므로.

options.text: His father’s blood has stopped the passage where those words should enter.
options.textKo: 아버지의 피가 그 말이 들어올 통로를 막아 버렸으므로.

options.text: Because he does not speak the boy’s language.
options.textKo: 그 아이의 말을 알아듣지 못하므로.

questions.sourceSnippet: my father’s blood Hath stopp’d the passage where thy words should enter

questions.question: How does Rutland turn that answer back on Clifford?
questions.questionKo: 러틀랜드는 그 답을 어떻게 되돌리는가?

options.text: He offers his own sword in his father’s place.
options.textKo: 아버지 대신 제 칼을 내민다.

options.text: He denies that his father killed Clifford’s father.
options.textKo: 아버지가 클리퍼드의 아버지를 죽였다는 것을 부인한다.

options.text: He calls on the soldiers to witness the murder.
options.textKo: 병사들에게 이 살해를 증언해 달라 부른다.

options.text: Then let his father’s blood open it again — "He is a man, and, Clifford, cope with him."
options.textKo: 그렇다면 제 아버지의 피가 그 통로를 다시 열게 하라며 — "그분은 어른이니, 클리퍼드여, 그분과 겨루시오."

questions.sourceSnippet: He is a man, and, Clifford, cope with him

questions.question: How far does Clifford say his revenge would have to go?
questions.questionKo: 클리퍼드는 제 복수가 어디까지 가야 한다고 말하는가?

options.text: Not until he roots out their accursed line and leaves not one alive — till then he lives in hell, for the sight of any of the house of York torments his soul.
options.textKo: 그 저주받은 혈통을 뿌리 뽑아 하나도 남기지 않을 때까지 — 그전에는 지옥에 사는 것이니, 요크 가문의 누구를 보아도 그의 영혼이 괴롭기 때문이라고.

options.text: Only until the Duke of York himself is dead.
options.textKo: 요크 공 한 사람이 죽을 때까지만.

options.text: Until the queen commands him to stop.
options.textKo: 왕비가 그만두라 명할 때까지.

options.text: He says his revenge is already satisfied.
options.textKo: 복수는 이미 다 이루어졌다고 한다.

questions.sourceSnippet: And till I root out their accursed line And leave not one alive, I live in hell

questions.question: On whose behalf does Rutland make his last appeal?
questions.questionKo: 러틀랜드는 마지막 호소를 누구를 걸고 하는가?

options.text: The queen, who he says would forbid it.
options.textKo: 이 일을 금하실 왕비.

options.text: Clifford’s own son — lest in revenge, since God is just, he be as miserably slain as Rutland.
options.textKo: 클리퍼드 자신의 아들 — 하느님이 공정하시니 그 되갚음으로 그 아들도 자기처럼 참혹히 죽지 않도록.

options.text: His brothers Edward and Richard.
options.textKo: 형들인 에드워드와 리처드.

options.text: The Tutor, who promised to answer for him.
options.textKo: 그를 대신해 답하겠다 한 가정교사.

questions.sourceSnippet: Thou hast one son; for his sake pity me

questions.question: What does Rutland offer instead of his life?
questions.questionKo: 러틀랜드는 목숨 대신 무엇을 제안하는가?

options.text: All his father’s lands in the north.
options.textKo: 북쪽에 있는 아버지의 영지 전부.

options.text: To carry Clifford’s challenge to the Duke of York.
options.textKo: 요크 공에게 클리퍼드의 도전장을 전하는 일.

options.text: To live in prison all his days, and to die only when he gives occasion of offence — for now Clifford has no cause.
options.textKo: 평생 감옥에 살다가 죄지을 일이 생겼을 때에만 죽겠다고 — 지금은 클리퍼드에게 아무 명분이 없으므로.

options.text: To renounce the name of Plantagenet for ever.
options.textKo: 플랜태저넷이라는 이름을 영영 버리는 것.

questions.sourceSnippet: Ah, let me live in prison all my days

questions.question: What is Clifford’s whole reason, stated at the last?
questions.questionKo: 마지막에 밝혀지는 클리퍼드의 이유 전부는?

options.text: That the queen has commanded the death of every York.
options.textKo: 왕비가 요크 사람은 모조리 죽이라 명했다는 것.

options.text: That Rutland tried to escape and so must die.
options.textKo: 러틀랜드가 달아나려 했으므로 죽어야 한다는 것.

options.text: That the boy carried arms against him in the field.
options.textKo: 그 아이가 전장에서 자기에게 무기를 들었다는 것.

options.text: "Thy father slew my father; therefore, die" — answering Rutland’s plea that the deed was done before he was born.
options.textKo: "네 아비가 내 아비를 죽였다. 그러니 죽어라" — 그 일이 자기가 태어나기도 전이었다는 러틀랜드의 호소에 대한 답으로.

questions.sourceSnippet: Thy father slew my father; therefore, die
